newsitem.title: SPAIN: Greek, Turkish action seen needed to back accord.
newsitem.headline: Greek, Turkish action seen needed to back accord.

text.p: An agreement between feuding NATO allies Greece and Turkey to improve relations was welcomed in both countries on Wednesday, but officials said action was now needed to back up the paper pledge.

A U.S.-brokered "convergence of views" issued on Tuesday at a NATO summit in Madrid committed Athens and Ankara to respect each other's rights and renounce use of force in their long- standing dispute over the Aegean Sea.
The document did not directly address the Aegean question or other points at issue between the Mediterranean neighbours, and U.S. officials called it a foundation for future action.

A Turkish foreign ministry spokesman said Ankara welcomed the set of six principles issued after Turkish Foreign Minister Ismail Cem and Greek counterpart Theodoros Pangalos met U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
"This conciliation meets most of our expectations. But the most important part of it now is implementation... otherwise documents do not mean anything by themselves," he said.
In Athens, government spokesman Nikos Athanasakis told reporters: "The Greek government considers this development highly positive and its adoption could open a new era in Greek-Turkish relations."
But he said Greece did not give up its right to extend its territorial waters from six to 12 miles in the Aegean, something that Turkey has called a cause for war.

The Greek stock market reacted favourably to the accord, rising 2.2 per cent in early trading. "News of a convergence of views between Greece and Turkey is adding life to the market," said Aris Eleftheriou, fund manager at Alpha Credit Bank's mutual fund arm.

Although Cyprus was not mentioned in the principles, U.S. officials said they hoped the accord would boost U.N.-sponsored talks opening in upstate New York on Wednesday between leaders of the divided Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities.
Cyprus is another key ingredient in the Greek-Turkish dispute, and developments there are strongly influenced by the atmosphere between Athens and Ankara.
The Aegean dispute is a complex tangle of overflight and seabed exploitation issues, partly stemming from the fact that many islands owned or claimed by Greece are close to the Turkish mainland.
The two countries almost went to war in January 1996 over an uninhabited islet known to Greeks as Imia and to Turks as Kardak, and were only held back by U.S. intervention.

Albright, who took office six months ago, has signalled a renewed U.S. interest in Greek-Turkish relations and the Cyprus problem, which are of key concern to Washington in its role as de facto leader of NATO.
She recently chose Richard Holbrooke, negotiator of the 1995 Dayton agreement on Bosnia, as U.S. special envoy for Cyprus to back up U.N. efforts for a settlement.
Analysts said Tuesday's declaration of principles, which was later endorsed by Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis and Turkish President Suleyman Demirel, was a careful balance of interests.

A clause barring "use of force or the threat of force" favoured Greece, while another clause committing both sides to recognise each other's "legitimate interests" in the Aegean met Turkish demands, they said.
U.S. officials said the agreement could only succeed if Greece and Turkey moved forward with practical solutions to outstanding problems.

They said such solutions could include working groups on various issues, deepening economic exchanges and a possible role for the Hague-based International Court of Justice in resolving some disputes.
